I just want to point out to the government that I would have thought there was nothing there at all; I would expect nothing at all. I was hoping that would have been the answer, that nothing of the kind had been done. I never recollect it being done. We have had questions of the same kind before, and we have had them answered, as I recollect, without any trouble at all, but the minister wishes to make this an order for a return. There are, I admit, lots of cases of refunds of the sales tax and the like, but in this case, unless the government say there are a lot of them, I see no reason why the question should not be answered. If the government say there are a lot of them, it is a different matter.

737404,ca.proc.d.1925-04-08.17.1.1.1.2,1925-04-08,f0d1049a-4acc-4789-a93f-b3bceae69e3f,ca.m.8624,Mr. WILLIAM IRVINE (East Calgary):,,THE BUDGET,CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL,MINISTER OF FINANCE.,"Mr. Speaker, at the time of the adjournment last night I was in the act of trying to balance the budget, a new kind of budget, a budget which shows a huge expenditure of promises, offset by a meagre income by way of fulfilment. During my attempt at balancing this budget I was interrupted by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock), while quoting a plank in the platform of the Liberal party made at the last election as an appeal to labour. The interruption was caused by my quoting clause 7 in the first half of the platform, which says:

column2: The principle that men and women should receive equal remuneration for work of equal value.

column1: The Minister of Labour said:

Does my hon. friend not know that neither this government nor the preceding government has had any authority in fixing the wages of civil servants, that authority being entrusted under a specific law to a commission which has exclusive jurisdiction in the matter?

Now I understand that while the government may not have full authority as the Minister of Labour suggests, it must oi necessity, according to the act referred to, give its approval to any proposal which the commission might make. If there are women civil servants who are not receiving the same salary as men in the civil service, has the government had any communication whatsoever with the commission in regard to that? Has the government made any effort at all to remove any such discrimination, if such discrimination exists?

I have one more suggestion to make in this regard: Supposing that what the Minister of Labour says is correct-namely, that the government has no authority to deal with the salaries of civil servants because of a certain act^-has not the government full power to change that act? Why not bring in an amendment now to this particular act limiting, if necessary, the power of the Civil Service Commission, or giving the government such power as the Minister of Labour thinks it ought to have?

I referred last night to the different accounts given by the various members of the cabinet at different times in this parliament as to the condition of the health of the nation. I showed that the government presented a picture which was suitable to the aims which it sought to gain for the moment. I would say that the government has applied the same
The Budget-Mr. Irvine

kind of reasoning to the balancing of its budget. As a matter of fact it has over-balanced the budget. It has balanced a certain expenditure over against a problematical income. It has ignored huge liabilities of the government in the case of the National railways merely in order that it may be able to make a pretence of balancing its budget. Now in view of the fact, Mr. Speaker, that there are some hon. gentlemen to follow me who would like to complete their speeches and get away for the Easter holidays I am not going to go into the details of the budget as I had prepared to do. As a matter of fact it is really unnecessary for me to do it, because other hon. members already have done so, and I have no doubt that many who will follow me will also deal with the budget in detail.

There are two main questions with respect to the budget that I want to comment on. I think that I may divide the main features of this budget into two questions. First, how can expenditure be reduced; is there any possible way by which we can further economize? The next question is; how is the revenue required to be raised? These are really the sum and substance of the budget. With regard to the first question-how can we economize?-while the government has protested time and time again its anxiety to economize, it has not told the people very frankly that the major portion of the public expenditures is really composed of fixed charges and that the largest item of the fixed charges is interest and that it cannot be reduced; no amount of economy by this or any other government can reduce that charge. The only way that that charge can be effectively altered would be to make some alteration not in the fiscal policy in so far as it applies to the tariff, but to make some such fundamental change as the control of public credit and finance.

How is the revenue to be raised is the next question? This brings us to the most contentious of all questions that arise in discussion of a budget, and that is the question of tariffs. At the present time we raise our revenue by tariffs, income tax and sales tax chiefly. Here I would just stop for a moment to protest against the Whole system of taxation that is applied in Canada at the present time. It is a duplication, it is unjust, it is expensive. Let me say further that I do not believe that there is any system of taxation which will ever solve the basic economic problems. The tariff is first of all as it is applied in Canada a means of collecting revenue. Secondly it might possibly be utilized as a protective agency to protect our industries; but I do not

see how we can effectively do both at the same time. For if we had a tariff that was sufficiently high to protect our industries it appears to me that it would not be a very good revenue producer. If, on the other hand, we have a tariff that is good at producing revenue I fail to see how it can be a protection to industry. I have just said that I do not regard the question of tariffs as being fundamental, in fact I do not think that any fiscal policy is fundamentally 'an economic question. I readily admit that any fiscal policy will have an effect upon the industrial life of the country. It will have an effect like the weather would have on one of the Petersen ships coming across the Atlantic say; if it blows hard it will retard the ship somewhat but it will likely get across; if it is a fair wind it can help her to make a more speedy passage. And so with the ship of state; the fiscal policy may retard a little or may increase the speed, but the fiscal policy is not a fundamental driving force. The tariff is the most contentious question however. It is in Canada of major importance in politics; it is universally, I think, of minor importance in economics. We have found that in Canada no party really stands for the abolition of a tariff. It is used by all parties largely as a means of producing revenue; and as I have just pointed out if the Conservative party were to carry its principles to their logical conclusion, as I understand it, we would have a protective tariff so high that it would not yield any revenue. If, on the other hand, the Liberal party were to take its own programme seriously and carry it into effect we would have free trade ultimately and consequently could not look to a tariff for any revenue. I am not charging the Liberal party, of course, with any free trade inclinations; but if ever it did have them, it has not furnished the country with any substitute proposal for collecting revenue. It seems to me that that is just one of the chief weaknesses of the Liberal party; it claims that it wishes to make towards free trade, but finding that it has no other means of collecting a revenue it just keeps on with the same old tariff in order to be able to balance the budget at the end of the year. It appears to me that the tariff as it is fixed now is possibly at the best level for producing revenue. If we had a Conservative government it would not raise the tariff very much higher providing that it aimed to use the tariff as a revenue producer. The present Liberal government, that has professed to revise the tariff downwards, will not revise it downwards very much more because if this were done the income would be depleted. And so we have a tariff fixed, as it appears to me, at that point
The Budget-Mr. Irvine
where it can produce the greatest amount of revenue. That is my view of the question.

We have therefore the worst evils of both systems in force in Canada at the present time. That is to say we have the worst evils that could come from partial free trade, the worst evils that could come from partial protection, and we have not obtained the inherent virtues of either of the philosophies that underlie this practice. Let me be a little more plain in what I mean by saying we have the worst evils of the two systems. As I have pointed out the tariff is not low enough to cheapen goods. That has been the claim of the Liberal party-that it wanted to reduce the tariff in order to reduce the price of goods to the consumer. But the tariff is not low enough to do that; on the other hand it is not high enough to be a protection to our industries. Everyone will agree that, in so far as it is a collector of revenue, it is a most expensive system. It has been estimated that by this method of collecting revenue three or more dollars go into somebody else's pocket for every one that goes into the treasury. It is not only a very expensive way of raising money, but it appears to me to be a very unjust way, and I think the agricultural industry more than any other bears the burden of the present system of tariff taxation. Next to the farming industry comes the average man or woman, the consumer, who may not be engaged, perhaps, in a protected industry at all, but must pay an extra .price for all protected goods. So that taking the tariff as it is today, this tariff that has been described as a moderate tariff is the most pernicious kind of a fiscal policy that any country could have. I wish to make the assertion that in my opinion the country can accommodate itself ultimately to any fiscal policy, providing that fiscal policy is stable. I think that a statement similar in character to that which I have just made was made in the budget debate in the British House of Commons by the former Premier, Lloyd George, just a few days ago. If further proof that a country can survive any fiscal policy were required, I would refer hon. members to Germany and to the United States. These countries have managed to survive, notwithstanding the fact that they have high protection. Next I will take you on the other side to Great Britain, as furnishing, I believe, the best example of a free trade country, and even Great Britain has managed to survive under free trade. But if you want the main outstanding example of all, I would point to Canada. Canada has been able to survive the worst kind of fiscal policy, a fiscal policy which I say is neither one thing nor 126

another. It is neither hot nor cold. The fiscal policy which we have now has been described as moderate. I think I can recall the former leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Crerar) referring to the tariff as an immoral thing. Now we have a moderate tariff, but if it is an immoral thing, let us be done with it. If it is not an immoral thing, let us use it; but as it is now I say it is a most unjust thing and a most expensive .method of raising the revenue of the country. It does not protect the industries. It does protect the manufacturer; that is to say it gives him an opportunity of charging a higher price for his goods, but it does not protect the industries, because it is never high enough to make them secure from the competition of the other countries. So that that is the tariff which we have now.

My contention then, Mr. Speaker, is that we must have one thing or the other. I am prepared with those hon. members opposite, to have free trade, if they are so prepared. But I think if any proof were needed more than we have had in the past we have it this year that they are not quite prepared to give the free trader anything approximating free trade. They are not even thinking about it, and I am not going to play ""pussy wants a comer"" with any government. If they are sincere about it, I am willing to give it a trial, because I believe if there is any science in government it must be experimental. But Canada has never experimented with anything like free trade,, and seeing now that there is no opportunity of even having a chance to experiment with it, I turn away from it to try some other experiment. I am not going to fool with it at all. The tariff as we have it now reminds me of that fable which speaks of a donkey starving to death standing between two haystacks. But remember, Mr. Speaker, that was merely a fable. A donkey would have more sense than that. Here we are with our tariff policy; no one seems to want to make it any lower, but simply to keep it as it is, destructive and stupid. Still we stand there. That is the reason why I am turning from that policy.

That brings me to the question asked by two hon. members to my right last night. They asked, why did I last year vote for a policy making towards free trade, while on this occasion I have indicated my opposition to a budget that was somewhat similar? That is a fair question and I want to take a little time to answer it. I want to make quite dear the attitude that I have assumed, whether it be right or wrong, on the question of tariff. I have just stated that I personally and the labour people whom I represent do not look
The Budget-Mr. Irvine

upon the tariff as being of fundamental and economic importance. In this we may be mistaken, but that is the attitude we take. Therefore I had no tariff platform at the last election. I was elected on an entirely different platform. The very first and most important point in my election-in fact it was the only thing-was that I was elected as a representative of labour, and that I was to consult with them from time to time as to their attitude on public questions. That was the only plank in my platform. I have just consulted with labour on this point. I did not fail to make inquiries of the Trades
column2: and

column1: Calgary and did not fail to make inquiry of the Labour party of Canada as to the attitude I should adopt on this question and I received their instructions. I am their delegate. If I cannot out of principle obey their instructions I should resign. But having the conviction myself that the question of the tariff will not solve the labour problem, having the conviction that we ought to try the one thing or the other, namely, free trade or protection and not something that is half way between them both, my course seems to me to be clear. Last year I still had a faint hope that there was a strong party in this House that stood for ultimate free trade, and that they were willing to take a step towards getting that free trade, and so when mj' hon. colleague brought in the resolution pointing that way I hoped, in fact I never doubted at that time, that that programme, being the programme of the Progressive party, would be supported by every one of them, and that it would be a challenge to the government that the next budget that came down would have to be a budget making towards free trade. For that reason I voted for it, because I am willing to try free trade if anybody else is. But this year, finding that nobody wants free trade, that nobody is even looking towards free trade, and realizing as I do that the tariff as it now stands is an objectionable thing, I turn my eyes towards the other side, and I ask, what has protection to give? Is protection going to be as timorous in its policy as free trade has been? If it is I must turn from it also. But at present I do not know that it is. There is the answer to the question my hon. friend put to me last night.

,Labour,,William Irvine,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=f0d1049a-4acc-4789-a93f-b3bceae69e3f&Language=E&Section=ALL

the confession of my hon. friend. I should have said that no party in this House stood for free trade. If I said ""no individual,"" I did not mean that. I believe there are still a few individuals who keep their first love burning bright, and all honour to them. I can understand them. But there is no major party in this House that seems to have any idea of standing for free trade.
Now I turn to the question of protection.

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to deal with a point which seems to me to be much more important than the tariff. I think it will be agreed that more and more the question of credit and finance is rising to the position of paramount consideration in all countries. The evidence of this comes from France just a day or two ago; I shall not, quote the despatch but I merely refer to it as bearing out my point that the question of the control of credit and of proper financing is becoming increasingly important. In a despatch of April 6, I note that Premier Herriot of France is asking for an increase of some two billion francs in the circulation of money, and is making it his policy to impose a capital levy of ten per cent. I do not know what the details of either of these policies are, nor do I say that either- of them is the right policy. I do say, however, that the fact that he is going to risk his government on a question of finance is proof to my mind that this question is becomnig a vital one for all nations to consider.

The government, are talking a good deal about prosperity. Sometimes they have found it to exist; sometimes they are only confident that we are going to get it. But surely they will agree that there can be no prosperity in
The Budget-Mr. Irvine

any country while a large percentage of its plant equipment is lying idle. There can be no prosperity in any country that lives largely on wages when a large percentage of the population are unemployed. There can be no prosperity in a country where the plant equipment and natural resources are unused. But how are we going to start these factories and get the men to work and utilize our natural resources? Some say we will do it by a certain kind of tariff policy. It may be so;

I do not think so. But I believe it can be done by a proper arrangement of national credit. So I make the suggestion to the government that they take one step in this direction; let the government begin by testing out this suggestion in a small way. At present the government hand the credit of the country over to financiers and borrow it back from them at a high rate of interest. Our interest account to-day amounts to nearly $200,000,000. which is more than comes in by the tariff. The government can save that much by proper financing. Let them begin by financing the next year the $400,000,000 or so that is required to meet the current expenditures by issuing that amount on the strength of the national credit instead of borrowing it from New York or some other p'aee. Having issued such credit instruments as may be required, they could balance the account at the end of the year by taxing to the extent of the amount issued. There wild be no inflation then-not any more than if they sold bonds; and they will save the entire amount they would have to pay out in interest. And I suggest that when they do their taxing they do not go to the sales tax or to the tariff or even to the income tax, but that they try out the single tax and see what the results would be. The single tax has at least the virtue of simplicity and of fairness. It would be required as much under a protective as a free trade policy as in either case revenue would be required. I will not expound that system of taxation, because I believe the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good), who is the best exponent of it in this House, will be dealing with the question when he speaks on the budget.. But I suggest that as one method of taxation that is better than either that is in use at present.

HUDSON (South Winnipeg):,,S, 1925",,,"Mr. Speaker, this session, as usual, the discussion on the budget has largely centred, around the tariff; and that, I suppose, is inevitable. I propose therefore to follow up the discussion, but in a somewhat different way from that which has been adopted by most members up to the present. Appeals have been made to the authority of political economists and to the experience of other countries, but very little has been said about the experience of our own country. It is with that experience that I propose to deal. In 1868, the first year after confederation, the total external

4 p.m. trade of Canada was $129,000,000, largely with the United States and the United Kingdom, just as it is now. At that time the tariff on all imported goods, whether free or dutiable, averaged 13.01 per cent. It fluctuated slightly but for the most part remained at about that figure until 1879. During the years following 1868 our external trade steadily increased; there were fluctuations, but on the whole the trend was upward until 1878 when it totalled $170,000,000. That year was a period of great business depression, and in 1879 our external trade dropped to $151,000,000, which was much lower than the average during the preceding ten years.

Now, the depression of 1878 began in the preceding year and continued through 1879, and naturally the people became uneasy; unemployment was general, industry ceased to operate, and large numbers of Canadians went to the United States and elsewhere. Our population in 1871 was 3,689,257, and the increase

during the decade was 635,553, making the population in 1881, 4,324,810. I have no means of ascertaining what the loss of population was by emigration; no doubt it was substantial, as it was before and as it has been since. But the public men of the time turned their attention to what they thought might be remedies for the situation, and in March 1878 Sir John Macdonald moved in the House of Commons an amendment to the budget, which was read 'by my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) the other day, and which I should like to read again:

That the Speaker do not now leave the chair but that this House is of the opinion that the welfare of Canada requires the adoption of National Policy, which by a judicious readjustment of the tariff will benefit and foster the agricultural, the mining, the manufacturing and other interests of the Dominion: that such a policy will retain in Canada thousands of our fellow countrymen who are now obliged to expatriate themselves in search of the employment denied them at home; will restore prosperity of our struggling industry now so sadly depressed; will prevent Canada from being made a sacrifice market; will encourage and develop an active interprovincial trade; and moving as it ought to do in the direction of reciprocity of tariffs with our neighbours so far as the varied interests of Canada may demand, will greatly tend to procure for this country eventually a reciprocity of trade.
Now, that is precisely the proposal which is suggested as a remedy for the existing situation in Canada.

column2: In the first period, that is from 1868

column1: to 1878, there was what was then called and what- might stall be called a revenue tariff, and there was a substantial increase in population and a moderate increase in trade. During the second period, that is from 1878 to 1896, there was what was called the protective tariff-what was adopted designedly as a protective tariff. During that period there was a small increase of population and an immense emigration, and there was stagnation in external trade. During the third period there was a slight lowering of tariffs, an immense increase in immigration and ia very large increase in external trade. The fourth period is the war period *with which I will not deal in detail. Now, my right hon. friend says ""Do you mean to say that the slight decreases in the average duties in 1897 or 1901 had the effect of creating this immense increase in trade, this immense immigration?"" I say that taking the figures as they stand alone I do not contend that it does. I do say this though, that one can easily underestimate the effect of a very slight marginal change in the price of a commodity. Sometimes a very slight change makes a tremendous difference 'in trade. My right hon. friend is probably familiar with the marginal theory of the mathematical economists.

as a matter of fact the trade which we have with one country comes under a lower tariff while the trade which we have with other countries is under a higher tariff you get nowhere at all by lumping the results together.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Arthur Meighen,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=d02a7b53-dad0-4944-82b0-aed9054a7bc2&Language=E&Section=ALL
737479,ca.proc.d.1925-04-08.18.66,1925-04-08,a9ef31d5-1519-4dcd-ac74-54f968693616,ca.m.6111,Mr. HUDSON:,,S, 1925",,,"Certainly you do. I will
leave with my right hon. friend the result of the facts I have given him. As I say, I do not contend that these changes in tariff were responsible for all the results. All that I

say is that at any rate, at the very least, the effect of those tariff changes was not to depress trade. What was the cause of the increased trade and increased immigration, apart from tariff? There are only two other causes that I can think of. The first is that there was a very vigorous and able administration in Canada. The second is that the world conditions were such that they encouraged the investment of large capital in Canada and therefore immigration to Canada.

That is all I wish to say in regard to tariff; but now our external trade has become more important to us than it ever was. Canada has become in trade matters a world nation, and one of the great nations of the earth, in regard to international commerce. From 1868 until 1916 our trade balance was continually against us, with an aggregate of two billion dollars. That meant that we were borrowing money in immense sums and were not even pajdng interest. So that now the aggregate debt of Canada to the outside world is variously estimated at from three and a half billions to five billions of dollars. That means that we have an immense interest bill to pay to the outside world, and how are we going to pay it? Heretofore, or prior to 1916, we paid it by borrowing more money. We cannot do that now. We have got to a point where we cannot afford to do it. We have to pay our interest bill. We have a mortgage on the farm and have to pay our interest bill out of our earnings, and we are doing it this year- probably we may do it in the future-by virtue of the farmer, the forest man and the fisherman. They are the people who are supplying us with eighty-five per cent of our external trade, and they are the people we have to consider in the future. We have got to have industries in this country, it is true, but we have got to have industries that can do a little more than pull their own weight in the boat. We cannot afford to have industries that can only survive by artificial support.

,Liberal,,Albert Blellock Hudson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=a9ef31d5-1519-4dcd-ac74-54f968693616&Language=E&Section=ALL
737524,ca.proc.d.1925-04-08.18.111,1925-04-08,efcd99fc-059e-4290-a7f4-bf960db25009,ca.m.8459,Mr. M. E. MAYBEE (Northumberland, Ont.):",,"S, 1925",,,"Mr. Speaker, Canada to-day is in

urgent need of some solution to our economic conditions that will bring about an industrial and agricultural awakening. This' fact is forcibly brought to my attention by the condition in my own constituency.

The county of Northumberland, which I have the honour to represent, is engaged in various industrial pursuits as well as mixed farming. I regret to have to report that various industries have been compelled to close their doors owing to unfair competition from imports, and others are struggling on, holding by a mere thread. For instance, we have a shoe company located in the town of Campbellford of fifty years' standing, and in this connection I desire to read a letter addressed to me, dated March 7, 1925:
M. E. Maybee, Esq., M.P.,
Parliament Buildings,
Ottawa, Ont.

Dear Sir,-In view of the depressed condition of trade through Canada, and the increasing importation of shoes from Great Britain, we are writing to ask you to use your influence for the purpose of attempting to remedy this condition of affairs.

We have been in business for 50 years and up until a couple of years ago our factory was run continuously without loss of a day's time. During the last two years, however, a change has been necessary, and particularly during the year that has just passed, we have only been able to give employment to our help for four days a week, and sometimes not even that.

You will easily see that this not only makes our help dissatisfied but also makes the cost of production very much greater, as instead of having steady production and a full week's time to carry our wages and overhead expenses, we are compelled to divide it over the four days in which we are working, and conditions are such that it seems impossible to make any headway.

We assure you that none in the shoe business is making excessive profits. During the past two years there have been a larger number of failures, we believe, than at any previous time. We, ourselves, lost more money during the past year than ever before.

We believe that if something can be done to remedy the present conditions so as to enable our workmen to work full time instead of losing time, as is being done at present, it will be a benefit to the workmen, to ourselves, and the general public, as things can then be produced at lower prices than they can be produced under present conditions.

Perhaps there is no necessity for us to write this to you as there is no doubt your influence would be exerted in the right direction in any case, but there will probably be no harm in keeping you informed as to the real conditions in the shoe trade.
Yours truly,
Richard Weston for
Weston Shoe Co. Ltd.

This is a striking illustration of the condition of the shoe industry. The statistics show that the quantity of shoes imported from Great Britain has increased 355 per cent in two years and 155 per cent in the last twelve months; a large quantity was also imported from Germany. Twenty more shoe factories have failed since the 1st of January, 1924. The wages paid to employees in Great Britain and Germany are much less than those paid here, and that consideration almost offsets the fifteen and three-quarter per cent preferential tariff on goods coming from Great Britain.

Another instance of the failure of industry in my constituency is that of the Cobourg Felt Company. The Cobourg Dye Company and the Cobourg Matting Company have been seriously affected by outside competition. Then, in the town of Trenton, adjoining my constituency, a very fine fertilizer plant has had to suspend operations due to the reductions in the duty on fertilizer. The Dominion Combing Mills in the same town have also had to struggle against the import of tops. Tops were imported during the year ending March 31st, 1924, according to the last trade returns available, to the amount of $4,047,674, and these came in free of duty. This concern is of great benefit to the farmers
The Budget-Mr. Maybee

of this community who are engaged in the production of wool. The closing of these industries or the reduction of their output ha3 had a great deal to do with the unemployment situation in my county and is also seriously affecting the home market for our agricultural products.

With respect to agriculture we have one of the finest counties in the province of Ontario. We have a varied production, including dairying, fruit growing, bacon hogs, poultry' products, vegetables, and beef cattle. Much interest is taken in dairying; our county has a good reputation in connection with the manufacture of butter and cheese. I think it would be preferable to have the cheese inspected and graded in the factories, from the point of view of the educational feature if for no other reason.
A great many dairy products are imported into Canada. According to the latest available trade returns the following milk products were imported during the year ending March 31, 1924:
Value
Milk and cream
Milk, condensed
Butter
Casein
Cheese
Total

I consider that the tariff on butter and cheese should be increased until it is at least equal to that of the United States, which is eight cents a pound on butter and five cents a pound on cheese as against four cents a pound on butter and three cents a pound on cheese coming into Canada.

Many of our herds are being tested for accreditation and are making a good showing. We have many splendid herds of pure bred cattle, and I regret the action of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) in lowering the scale of compensation.

Our county is one of the foremost in the province in the production of apples, as well as of numerous small fruits, having secured a wide reputation in many international exhibitions. Here again we are labouring under a decided disadvantage, owing to climatic conditions, especially in small fruits, as the United States growers, under natural conditions, can produce fruits much earlier than we can and by the time our fruits are on sale the markets are surfeited with United States fruits and our growers never get the top prices. According to the trade returns for the fiscal year
ending March 31, 1924, the imports of fruit during that year were as follows:
Value of Import
Apples (fresh)
Apricots and quinces
Bananas
Wild berries
Berries
Cherries
Cranberries
Currants
Grapefruit
Grapes
Lemons
Melons
Oranges
Peac&es
Pears
Pineapples
Plums
Strawberries
Other fruits

The total imports of fresh fruits from the British Empire was valued at $169,153, and of fresh fruits from foreign countries, $18,084,294. Total fruits including dried and canned fruits from the British Empire amounted to $774,683, and from foreign countries, $25,760,319. A great many of these fruits we ourselves can produce. A sufficient duty should be imposed to safeguard the Canadian market until Canadian fruit is available. I believe the fruit growers of Northumberland and Durham, as well as other organizations, have made representations to the government for relief, and I trust that these will be acted upon.

As a sideline with dairying, bacon hogs are being produced in considerable quantities in Northumberland. I think in this the grading system is producing beneficial results and while not yet perfect no doubt it will eventually attain success. We can produce just as good bacon as Denmark, and while the education of our producers may be slow, it will eventually be completed. Another sideline with dairying is the development of poultry products. Some are specializing in this line. Here again we are under a great handicap, accentuated largely by climatic conditions and lack of protection. Recently seven car loads of eggs arrived in Montreal on one day, and the effect was immediately felt in our market. While we are producing poultry under winter conditions, these products are being shipped in here from the south where they are produced under summer conditions. We impose a tariff of only 3 cents per dozen against them, while they charge 8 cents per dozen against ours. We find at the same time that eggs were imported for consumption to the value of $1,975,707, which includes $12,679 worth from Hong Kong, China. Adequate protection should be given the production of
The Budget-Mr. Maybee
day-old chicks. I believe that something over

1,000,000 of such chicks came into Canada last year. Rigid inspection should take place at the border for not only the European fowl pest but for all contagious diseases affecting fowl. The grading of eggs is imposing considerable hardship on the producer. Many local dealers are refusing to handle them altogether, due to the extra labor entailed, thereby curtailing the local market, and as the salaries of the inspectors for the last fiscal year were $42,112, some real advantage to the producer should be shown.

A great many potatoes, vegetables and garden stuffs are produced in Northumberland, and here we find unfair competition from United States imports, due to their climatic conditions, American products flooding our markets much earlier than we can produce the vegetables. I find for the same period that I quoted before we imported the following vegetables:
Value
Cabbage
Onions dutiable
Onions free
Potatoes
Tomatoes
Other vegetables

The total value of fresh vegetables imported from the British Empire amounted to $154,375, while from foreign countries our imports reached the huge total of $3,777,881. All of these vegetables could have been grown in Canada. Total vegetables during the same period including dried, canned and pickled vegetables from the British Empire to the value of $574,816, and from foreign countries, $4,904,884. While the grading of potatoes generally may be advisable, I see no reason why a market gardener, selling produce on a local market direct from producer to consumer, where the buyer can see what he is buying and in most cases knows the seller, should be obliged to grade and tag the commodity, thereby entailing considerable labour and expense.

The conditions existing in the county 1 represent apply very largely to Canada as a whole. There is a general demand throughout Canada for a consistent application of the tariff; first, for the raising of revenue, thereby obviating the necessity of objectionable direct taxation; and second, sufficient protection to stabilize our industrial and agricultural activities. A policy to develop our own natural resources is urgently required. From the port of Cobourg alone in my constituency, according to an answer to a ques-

tion I placed on the order paper, in the fiscal years 1922, 1923, 1924 and 5 p.m. up to February 28, 1925, 264,239-cords of pulpwood were exported. At $10 per cord this represents a value of $2,642,390. If we had exported this pulpwood in the form of newsprint, we would have received $18,496,730, and at least $13,211,950 would have gone into the pockets of Canadian workmen.

We would not know of the excellent conditions prevailing in Canada if we had not been told by the Prime Minister and his colleagues during their meanderings up and down this country. We do not require any novel ideas for constructive legislation today. Conditions are very similar to those-of 1878, when the citizens of Canada decided by their franchise to inaugurate a National Policy to protect the industries and the people of this country. If they were wise in 1878, it does not take a great deal of acumen to see what would1 be wise in this present day. The depreciation of currency; the low cost of labour; the ruin of Europe-these things have exposed our markets in all directions, whether industrial or agricultural, to a competition that cannot survive under ordinary conditions. The question confronting us to-day is, what does Canada need to establish an atmosphere of confidence and prosperity? Something to encourage the investment of capital, primarily. Undoubtedly we need more population to assist us in our expenditure and produce commodities for railway transportation, but what folly to expend huge sums for immigration when we are unable to assimilate newcomers. British and American investors are awaiting the opportunity of consistent investments. But When thousands of industries have recently closed their doors, they do not appeal to these investors as consistent investments.

The present government is like a weather vane, constantly changing front according to the wind, promising all things to all people. As some of the people can be fooled all of the time, they have succeeded to that extent; but I believe the citizens of Canada are waiting for the opportunity to rise up in their might, as they did in 1911, and demand a sane policy for Canada. I do think that the situation in Canada at the present time is one which demands the most careful and earnest consideration of all classes of the people. I think we all agree that it is a grave one. There is a vein of discontent and of pessimistic feeling which is quite apparent as one travels through the country or listens to speeches made in the two Houses of Par-

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Milton Edgar Maybee,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=efcd99fc-059e-4290-a7f4-bf960db25009&Language=E&Section=ALL

737526,ca.proc.d.1925-04-08.19.1.1,1925-04-08,,,,stagedirection,,,,"The Budget-Mr. Brown

Lament; and there is also a buoyant and optimistic feeling, which refuses to lapse into pessimism-a feeling that if proper conditions are made to prevail the future of Canada is safe. The public debt has been increasing by millions since the war. Diminished indirect revenues mean greater direct taxation. The United States have greatly reduced their income tax, making this a greater incentive for investors to invest in United States. Other nations have reduced taxation and their indebtedness. We cannot live upon sentiment, and the average individual to-day does not believe he is prosperous unless he can see the actual returns for his labours. Sir Wilfrid Laurier once said in 1899 that if he became premier the people would not need statistics to tell them they were prosperous-""they would have the money in their pockets."" The Prime Minister is trying to show we are wealthy by arithmetic, but all the figures in creation will not convince the Canadian people that they are prosperous because ""they have not the money in their pockets."" I think it was the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) who said: ""Our unemployed are crying for bread and the premier gives them statistics.""

To sum it all up we must have protection for all our activities. The hon. member for Queens (Mr. Mackinnon) referred to the British embargo on potatoes, which he considered an injustice. Great Britain also had an embargo on cattle. But I would direct the hon. member's attention to the fact that that is the most effective means of protection. While Great Britain's fiscal policy is generally known as the nearest approach to free trade of that of any nation, she does not hesitate to protect her agriculturists or her industrialists if found necessary.

The tariff is a weapon to defend ourselves, or an equalizer of conditions; a means whereby we can demand and get consideration in our trade agreements. It resolves itself into one of two things, either protection or annexation. The reduction on farm implements has proven to be a fiasco so far as any benefit to the farmer is concerned. As has been shown in this House:
Binders are $2 higher now than in 1921; disc drills. $10 higher; cultivators, $3 higher; harrows, $1.50 higher; disc harrows, $4 higher.
Production of farm machinery is greatly reduced, fully 50 per cent in 1924, partially due to the tariff, and partially due to general conditions and the present buying power of the farmer.
The fact that the government in their budget are proposing to raise the duty on a certain class of coal, goes to show that they

recognize the fallacy of a free-trade policy, and the need of protecting our own resources, thereby admitting the wisdom of the national policy of protection. Canada is suffering from an impotent administration and until the sentiment of my right hon. leader's (Mr. Meighen) resolution is adopted will continue to suffer.
In conclusion, I wish to quote the words of Solomon in Proverbs XXIX, 2: ""When the righteous are in authority the people rejoice, but when the wicked beareth rule the people mourn.""",,,,

BROWN (Lisgar):,,"S, 1925 19S9",,,"Mr. Speaker, it was not my thought until a few minutes ago to take part in this debate at this time, but I thought that perhaps I might profitably, or unprofitably as the case may be, use up a few of the minutes that are left between now and six o'clock. There are a few thoughts that I would like to express on the budget that has been brought down, and on some of the questions that have been made matters of controversy.

In regard to the railway situation and the railway debt forming part of the debt of the country as a whole, it seems to me very desirable at the present time that there should be a distinction made in the two accounts. Some of us, of course, have very strongly advocated that the capitalization of the railways should be placed at its proper figure and the additional amount, of course, would be added to the ordinary debt of the country. Pending the coming of that time, it seems to me desirable that there should be a clear distinction made between our railway debt and the ordinary debt of the country. We all recognize that it really does not make any difference in the end, and it seems to me there has been a good deal of argument about things as to which there is in reality no difference of opinion. But still I can see some reasons why it is desirable that the two debts should be kept distinct. The railway obligations were incurred in a special manner, and apart from the ordinary financing of the country, and if the time comes when a portion of that should be put over against the consolidated debt of the country, I think it should be made very clear and distinct how much of the debt has been incurred because of our railway obligations. Therefore, until the time comes when we have done that, it seems to me very desirable that we should separate the two accounts. Indeed, I think it would be well if we could separate our accounts still further. I think it would be well if we had a clear and definite statement, or as near as possible as
The Budget-Mr. Brown

it can be arrived at, of the debt that properly should be attributed to the war. That would enable us and those who come after us to know just what sacrifices Canada made in regard to the war, and know just how much of the debt was incurred, because of the situation in which we found ourselves in regard to the railways.

As regards the other matter that has been in dispute, the question of the so-called surplus, I must say that notwithstanding all that has been said to justify the statement that was made by the hon. Acting Minister of Finance, (Mr. Robb), I cannot persuade myself that that particular account in regard to Roumania and Greece is anything more than possibly a good asset, possibly a better secured asset than it was before. Nevertheless that amount should not have been counted as either revenue or surplus.

There is one other matter that has been referred to and upon which I would like to express a few thoughts, and that is on the export of electrical power. I thought perhaps the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) would deal with a phase of the matter I have in mind when he spoke, but he did not do so.

So far as the exporting of power in itself is concerned, and the taking of a revenue therefrom, I would have no objection to that if it would not possibly involve us in difficulties in the future. I can well understand how the adoption of the principle of exporting power might possibly build up in the United States industries that depended upon that power, and if the time came, as we would all like it to come, when we would need all that power for ourselves, we might then very well find that vested interests had been created, and that we could not interfere with the export of power without creating a great deal of friction between ourselves and our neighbours to the south. I would therefore urge the utmost caution in that regard, for it seems to me that in this particular case we might possibly find ourselves involved in a situation that would be fraught with difficulties.

There are two or three things that I want to say in regard to the propositions that are being advanced by those who are traditionally the protectionist party. There have already been a good many gibes thrown at them over their panacea for every ill, but perhaps I may be pardoned for making another. About fifty yars ago or more, there was a craze in the Old Country in regard to the so-called curative properties of blue glass. It was supposed that if people could only live under blue glass they would be

cured from almost any disease. There was a popular comic song that went the rounds of the music halls about it; and I know it got as far as the prairies forty years ago through an ex-music hall singer. I can only remember a little bit of it, but one line went something like this:
column2: Put a single baby in

column1: a blue glass cradle, and it's sure to turn to twins,"" and the refrain went like this:
Blue glass, blue glass, '
The great discovery sure,
If you ever get sick You can cure it up quick By trying the blue glass cure.
It seems to me some such thought is behind the idea of those who advocate that high protection will be a cure for all our diseases and a remedy for all our economic ills.

I w'ould like to pay a little attention to some of the things that were said by the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion). I am sorry he is not here, but as I may not have an opportunity of speaking in his presence, I will have to say what I have to say now. Some time ago, in the early part of this session, the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River undertook to prove that the tariff was not always a tax, and I should like to criticize some of the arguments that he used to support his contention. I only hope that the hon. member in question is a better doctor than he is a logician, and that for the sake of his patients he is more correct in his diagnoses than he is when he undertakes to handle some of these tariff matters in the House of Commons. You will remember that he undertook to prove that a tariff was not a tax by citing facts that were given by Mr. F. W. Stewart of Montreal. He cited the statement that certain articles of clothing were higher priced in the United States than they are in Canada. At the time I called his attention to the fact that a proper comparison would have been one made between the prices in Great Britain and in Canada. He certainly does not do anything to prove his point when he quotes the prices in Canada and compares them with prices in a country where they have still higher protection. So far as proving his point is concerned the hon. gentleman absolutely falls down. The tariff is a tax on us if the price that we have to pay is greater than we can secure the article for from the cheapest source of supply not from a country so highly protected as the United States. Where in that case was the tax that the Prime Minister states the tariff is? In 1878, four years after that, steel rails cost only $39 a ton or about one-quarter of what they cost in 1867. In 1885, still under the same tariff, they were costing $27 a ton, at which price they practically remained until prior to the war.

Now when a person undertakes to deal with a problem he must take all the factors of the problem into account and unless the hon. member can show us that the prices in other places where they make rails were greater than in the United States-I have not the figures for the rails that migjht have been procured in Great Britain and Germany at the time-his argument fails. I contend it is up to the hon. gentleman to show us that $27 a ton, was less than steel rails could be procured for in other places, and until he can show that he certainly has not proved his point that the tariff is not a tax.

The hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) was a little exercised over this matter yesterday and he instanced and just as illogically the duty that is levied by the United States against our wheat. He wants to know who pays the duty. Well, for practical purposes, there is no duty paid by anybody. When the wheat enters the United States there is a duty paid and it is rebated when the flour is exported with very few exceptions. In that case, however, there is no duty paid, and if under the present conditions of the grain trade with the prices prevailing in Canada and the United States a small portion of that wheat enters the United States for consumption the United States consumer undoubtedly pays the duty. But so far as wheat is concerned nobody pays the duty at the present time to all practical purposes because it is rebated. Personally I have never been one, certainly for very many years, who has argued that the consumer pays the duty under all circumstances. That will depend in the first instance very largely upon where the market is made. If we are in a position to fix the prices, if the market is fixed here on the things that we import, then possibly we may find ourselves in a position to secure part of the duty from those who export to us; but that simply is not the case in regard to the great mass of Canadian imports and speaking generally, and with very few exceptions so far as Canada is concerned, the consumer pays the duty, because we are not in a position to exercise any very great in-127

He simply made the statement that these commodities could be produced in Canada. Now, I took only a few items from the list that he quoted at that time, I only had time to go into those although possibly I might have found something very interesting if ! had looked up some of the others. But if you turn up the speech of the hon. member (Mr. Manion) you will find that in the list of goods he quoted as goods which could be produced in Canada there were $25,000,000 worth of fruit. Now, in that respect I contend that I have been very liberal, and I have included $379,000 worth of melons. Will anybody seriously contend that Canada could produce the melons that come into Canada, both in eastern Canada and in the northwest, in many carloads? It may be contended that we should not use them, that we should exclude them, but no person would seriously contend that we could produce them in Canada. We can produce melons in Canada; we know that, but not in the quantities in which they are imported. The same may be said in regard to grapes. I find here an amount of $874,000, and yet we know that the Canadian fresh grapes are only on the market a very short time; therefore I imagine that that $874,000 is in very large measure made up of fruit that simply cannot be produced in Canada. We might say the same thing in regard to the $220,000 of cranberries, and possibly some of the other things as well. That is, the fresh fruit.
Now in regard to dried fruits I think I have been equally liberal in this matter. The figures are as follows:

That is for fresh fruits and dried fruits a total of $6,798,000. I am almost disposed to use some of the harsh language in regard to the hon. member for Fort William ancf Rainy River that he used in regard to the Acting Minister of Finance. There was another item in the list I gave that goes to make up the total of $27,000,000, in which I could not very well segregate those that might be produced in Canada from the total, and that is fruits otherwise prepared. But the total was less than $2,000,000. No person would seriously contend that Canada should cease the importation of oranges, bananas, grapefruit and melons. These contribute to and are necessary for the health of our people and are imported in large quantities, and we would continue to import them in large quantities even if a protectionist party should come into power.

The excess of imports over exports of raw hides is $1,643,334. But we must consider the reason for the importation of these hides. What is the reason? Many of those raw hides that are imported are of varieties used only in the manufacture of such light leather wear as gloves, and so forth, which we do not produce in Canada. Then we must remember the situation as regards tanneries in the city of Kitchener. There are some large tanneries there. I am given to understand that those tanneries do not use a pound of Canadian hides. Now why? Because Canadian hides are not of a quality that suits their purpose. If Canadian hides were of a quality that suited their purpose, would these men go away down to the Argentine and bring hides from that country? It will be noted if these returns are examined that the great bulk of these cattle skins, the heavy hides, come from the Argentine and from the United States, and I think likely from the southern states, from the hot climates. I am given to understand by those who are familiar with this subject, that the cattle from the warm climates produce a heavier hide, more suitable for sole leather and heavy leather belting than our northern hides-that our northern hides are simply not suitable for this purpose. These tanneries import these cattle skins to the amount of $4,771,284. What do they do with the hides. They tan them and export them. It is surely good protectionist doctrine, is it not, to encourage industry, and to encourage
The Budget-Mr. Brown

manufacturers, and surely these gentlemen who would advocate the exclusion of the hides or the putting of an impossible duty upon them, would not go so far as to deprive their factories that they are so fond of talking about of their raw product which it is necessary for them to have in order to continue operations.

What about the unmanufactured leather they export? These tanneries export leather to the amount of $5,633,581, and we import leather to the amount of $4,170,628. That means that there is an excess of exports over imports of $1,462,953, and remember that in those imports of leather are also large amounts that are made up of dressed glossed leather of various kinds that is not produced in Canada at all. So that the result of putting an embargo or a high protective duty against these hides from South America and from the United States would be that the tanneries- and I am told there are two very large ones in Kitchener, I understand among the largest in America.-would be compelled to go out of business, because they could not get the raw product. That is the way our hon. friends to my right want to help some of our manufacturers.

But there is another figure here which is somewhat interesting. We exported to the United States $4,163,278 worth of leather and we imported from the United States $3,342,616 worth. That means an excess of exports over imports of leather to the United States of $S20.662. I would advise the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River and the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland), who is frequently harping upon this matter, to search into some of these things a little more closely afad just see what would be the result of the application of the principle that they wish to apply as a remedy for ail evils of the body politic.

Another matter I thought of dealing with has been dealt with so ably by the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Lapierre) that 1 do not think I will say much in regard to it. I refer to the question of the export of pulpwood and the placing of an embargo on the export of pulpwood. The hon. member who spoke on that subject has evidently given a great deal of thought to it, and I admit he is much more competent to speak with authority on it than I can be since he is intimately in touch with it, but he expressed admirably the sentiments that I hold in regard to it. The weakness of those who advocate the embargo lies in this that they tangle it up with the principle of conservation. They tell us, when we express opposition to an embargo, that new pulpmills coming in would take care of the products of 127i

the forests, of the interests of the backwood settlers, by the establishment of new mills. Then, as regards the conservation of the forests, it does not make a particle of difference whether that pulpwood is used by the mills we have in Canada or by the American mills where they are to-day. I listened with a great deal of interest to the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Dickie) when he was speaking on this question the other night, and my attitude towards this whole question of forest conservation is intensely sympathetic. To me, there is no greater tragedy than to go through the great devastated areas that we see between here and Winnipeg, through British Columbia and along the Pacific coast. It is one of the greatest tragedies that we could possibly witness, and the generation that comes after us will hold as an account against us that we have been so prodigal in dissipating the tremendous timber resources that we fell heir to. So when I speak on this matter, I speak as one who cannot go to cut down a tree without feeling some qualms of conscience over it, because we live in a country where there are not very many trees. When I listened to the hon. member for Nanaimo, speaking sometimes almost with tears in his voice,-and I sympathized with him-of the destruction of our forests on the one hand and then, on the other, speaking with enthusiasm of the great manufacturing plants growing up on the Pacific coast that would take care of all the logs that cou'.d be cut, I wondered where he stood in the matter. The only remedy that will be useful in the conservation of timber is simply to cease cutting timber, and there is no more important duty that this parliament is faced with than that of devising some well-considered policy of conservation, fire protection and reforestation. This is a duty for parliaments, for governments. It is true that here and there are individuals who have done a ereat deal of valuable work in reforestation. But it is only the exceptional individual who will plant a forest for the benefit of posterity. This is a work that must be done by governments, and for my part I am prepared to support a very much larger appropriation than has ever yet been made for the prevention of fire and for the reforestation of those areas of Canada that have been so sadly swept by fire.",,,,

737538,ca.proc.d.1925-04-08.21.7,1925-04-08,b1d5c682-1934-44e3-8c98-235be860bb63,ca.m.3501,Mr. BROWN:,,$ 878,415 105,443 12,304 21,627 105,978 220,013 874,941 379,467 REVISED EDITION",,,"If it had the effect, as it might well have, of enabling us on the prairies to get cheaper lumber, perhaps we might be forgiven. The other day the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) depicted the conditions in which the miners were living. I was thinking-and many of us can testify to this-that there are thousands of people in the western provinces who, because of the high prices of lumber, made high by the high freight rates, and because immense quantities of timber that we sometimes think we ought to have a share of, are shipped to foreign countries, are at present unable to buy timber to make comfortable homes for themselves or for their cattle. Therefore, if we are going to talk about the principle ol embargoes on exports or even export duties, we should take into account the question of export duty on rough lumber. After all, how much difference is there between shipping a log and shipping timber that has been sawn on four sides? I found out when I was at Vancouver a year ago that practically all the timber shipments to Japan are simply rough sawn. I am told that the logs are dressed down, sized a little. After all, there is not much difference between shipping a log and shipping a piece of timber sawn on four sides. The amount of labour involved in putting it into that condition is pitifully small.

There is another matter to which I should like some of our friends who are opposed to the exportation of raw material to give a little thought. A little pamphlet came into our hands yesterday, evidently sent to us by a good protectionist, and I wish to refer to this passage in it. It was pointed out that Canada exports to the United States five
(Mr. Brown.]

cents worth of timber and the United States takes that and makes a chair worth five dollars. Of course, the argument is that we should make all those chairs at home. It is like the old argument that we should turn a ton of steel into watch-springs and how much more valuable the steel would be if we would put enough work on it to turn it into watch-springs. The argument in this little pamphlet was evidently that we should manufacture all our lumber into chairs. When I read that I remembered what a former member of this House, a furniture manufacturer, told me a few weeks ago. He said that there were enough furniture factories in Canada to make furniture for twenty million people. If that statement is true, hon. members can see the absurdity of pointing out, as an argument against the export of our raw material, that the United States make $4.95 out of our five cents worth of lumber. These are some of the absurdities into which hon. gentlemen are led when they pursue their policy, as they evidently intend to pursue it, to the extreme.
